items.title: I can describe the principle of mass spectrometry
items.what: Mass spectrometry works by vaporising a sample, ionising its molecules by bombarding them with high-energy electrons, accelerating the resulting ions through an electric field, and then separating them by mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) using a magnetic field before detecting them.
items.why: Understanding the principle allows you to interpret why different compounds produce different spectra and why the technique is so sensitive and specific for identification purposes.
items.example: An ethanol molecule (M) loses an electron to form M+ (the molecular ion). This M+ ion may then fragment further, for example losing a CH3 group to give a fragment at m/z = 31.

subtopic.name: Mass Spectrometry
subtopic.what: Mass spectrometry (MS) is an analytical technique that ionises molecules and separates the resulting ions based on their mass-to-charge ratio (m/z). The data is displayed as a spectrum of relative intensity versus m/z, revealing the molecular mass and fragmentation pattern of a compound.
subtopic.why: Mass spectrometry allows chemists to identify unknown compounds, determine molecular masses with high precision, and analyse complex mixtures such as blood samples in drug testing or trace substances at forensic crime scenes. It is one of the most powerful tools for compound identification in modern analytical chemistry.

items.title: I can define the base peak in a mass spectrum
items.what: The base peak is the tallest peak in a mass spectrum, assigned a relative intensity of 100%. All other peaks are expressed as a percentage of the base peak's intensity.
items.why: The base peak represents the most stable or most abundant fragment ion produced during ionisation. Recognising it allows you to read the relative intensity scale correctly and identify major fragments.
items.example: In the mass spectrum of ethanol, the base peak appears at m/z = 31, which corresponds to the [CH2OH]+ fragment ion. It is the tallest peak and is given a relative intensity of 100%.

items.title: I can define the molecular ion peak in a mass spectrum
items.what: The molecular ion peak is the peak with the highest m/z value in the spectrum (furthest to the right), representing the intact molecule that has lost one electron to form M+. It corresponds to the molecular mass of the compound.
items.why: The molecular ion peak directly gives the molecular mass of the compound, which is an essential first step in identifying an unknown substance from its mass spectrum.
items.example: Ethanol (C2H5OH) has a molecular mass of 46 g/mol, so its molecular ion peak appears at m/z = 46 in the mass spectrum.

items.title: I can identify the base peak and molecular ion peak from a given mass spectrum
items.what: From a displayed mass spectrum, the molecular ion peak is identified as the peak at the highest m/z value, while the base peak is identified as the peak with the greatest relative intensity (height of 100%).
items.why: Being able to locate these two key features is the foundation of all mass spectrometry data analysis and is required before any further interpretation can take place.
items.example: In a mass spectrum showing peaks at m/z = 15, 29, 31, and 46, with the peak at m/z = 31 being the tallest: m/z = 46 is the molecular ion peak and m/z = 31 is the base peak.

items.title: I can state that the molecular ion peak corresponds to the molecular mass of the compound
items.what: The m/z value of the molecular ion peak is equal to the molecular mass of the compound in g/mol, because the molecular ion M+ carries a charge of +1 (z = 1), making m/z = m/1 = m.
items.why: This relationship allows you to directly read off the molecular mass from the spectrum and use it to confirm or determine the molecular formula of the compound.
items.example: A compound with a molecular ion peak at m/z = 60 has a molecular mass of 60 g/mol. This is consistent with ethanoic acid (CH3COOH), which has M = 60 g/mol.

items.title: I can determine the ions that correspond to fragments in a given mass spectrum
items.what: Fragment peaks arise when the molecular ion breaks apart at bond positions. You can identify a fragment by calculating masses of possible sub-groups (e.g. CH3 = 15, C2H5 = 29) or by subtracting the fragment's m/z from the molecular ion m/z to find what was lost.
items.why: Fragment identification provides structural information about where bonds exist in the molecule and what groups are present, adding detail beyond what the molecular mass alone can reveal.
items.example: Hexane (C6H14, M = 86) shows a peak at m/z = 71. Since 86 - 71 = 15, this represents the loss of a CH3 group. The fragment ion is [C5H11]+.

items.title: I can determine the identity of a compound from given mass spectrometry data
items.what: By reading the molecular ion peak to obtain molecular mass and comparing it to the molecular masses of possible candidate compounds, the identity of an unknown can be determined. Fragment peaks can provide additional confirmation.
items.why: This is the practical application of all mass spectrometry skills and is directly examined in VCE. It demonstrates how MS data translates into a real identification conclusion.
items.example: A spectrum shows a molecular ion peak at m/z = 60. Since pentane (C5H12) has M = 72 and 2-methylbutane also has M = 72, but ethanoic acid has M = 60, the compound is identified as ethanoic acid.

items.title: I can describe the principle of infrared spectroscopy
items.what: Different chemical bonds absorb infrared radiation at characteristic frequencies (wavenumbers). When IR radiation is passed through a sample, bonds absorb energy at their specific frequencies and vibrate more, and the absorbed frequencies appear as troughs (low transmittance) in the resulting spectrum.
items.why: Understanding the principle explains why different functional groups appear at predictable positions in the spectrum, making it possible to use wavenumber tables to identify bond types systematically.
items.example: The O-H bond in an alcohol absorbs IR radiation strongly in the range 3200-3600 cm-1. When ethanol is analysed, a broad trough appears in this region, confirming the presence of a hydroxyl group.

subtopic.name: Infrared Spectroscopy
subtopic.what: Infrared (IR) spectroscopy identifies the types of chemical bonds present in a molecule by measuring which wavelengths of infrared radiation are absorbed. The spectrum is displayed as transmittance (%) versus wavenumber (cm-1), with absorption appearing as downward troughs.
subtopic.why: IR spectroscopy is widely used to identify functional groups in organic compounds, confirm the purity of synthesised products, and detect substances in forensic and environmental analysis. It is a fast, non-destructive technique that provides clear evidence for the presence or absence of specific bond types.

items.title: I can identify bond types present in a sample from given infrared spectroscopy data
items.what: By comparing the wavenumber positions of absorption troughs in a spectrum against a reference table of characteristic absorption ranges, you can identify which bond types are present. The absence of a trough in a particular range can also rule out certain functional groups.
items.why: Identifying bond types from IR data is a core analytical skill that provides direct evidence for the functional groups in a molecule, which in turn constrains what the compound can and cannot be.
items.example: An IR spectrum shows troughs at approximately 2950 cm-1 (C-H bond, 2850-3090 cm-1) and 1735 cm-1 (C=O bond, consistent with an ester at 1720-1840 cm-1), but no broad trough at 2500-3500 cm-1, ruling out a carboxylic acid O-H.

subtopic.name: Infrared Spectroscopy
subtopic.what: Infrared (IR) spectroscopy identifies the types of chemical bonds present in a molecule by measuring which wavelengths of infrared radiation are absorbed. The spectrum is displayed as transmittance (%) versus wavenumber (cm-1), with absorption appearing as downward troughs.
subtopic.why: IR spectroscopy is widely used to identify functional groups in organic compounds, confirm the purity of synthesised products, and detect substances in forensic and environmental analysis. It is a fast, non-destructive technique that provides clear evidence for the presence or absence of specific bond types.

items.title: I can determine the identity of organic compounds from provided options using given infrared spectroscopy data
items.what: When given a set of possible compounds and an IR spectrum, you eliminate candidates by checking which bond types should be present or absent. The compound whose expected absorption pattern matches the observed spectrum is the correct identification.
items.why: This is a key exam skill in VCE Chemistry. The process of elimination using IR data, particularly using the absence of expected peaks, is often more decisive than confirming peaks that may overlap.
items.example: A compound with formula C4H8O2 shows a C=O trough at 1740 cm-1 but no broad O-H trough at 2500-3500 cm-1. This rules out a carboxylic acid and confirms it is an ester, since esters have C=O (1720-1840 cm-1) but no O-H absorption.

items.title: I can explain the role of the fingerprint region in IR spectroscopy
items.what: The fingerprint region spans 500-1500 cm-1 and contains a complex, unique pattern of absorption bands resulting from the combined vibrations of all atoms in the molecule. Like a human fingerprint, it is unique to each compound.
items.why: The fingerprint region is used as a confirmatory test to verify the identity of a compound by comparing its spectrum with a reference library spectrum. It is especially useful when functional group analysis alone is insufficient to distinguish between similar compounds.
items.example: Two different isomers may both show C=O and C-H absorptions in the functional group region, but their fingerprint regions (500-1500 cm-1) will differ, allowing them to be distinguished when compared against known reference spectra.

items.title: I can describe the principle of nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy
items.what: NMR spectroscopy places a sample in a strong magnetic field, causing certain atomic nuclei (such as 13C or 1H) to align with or against the field. A radiofrequency pulse causes the nuclei to absorb energy and flip their alignment, and as they relax back they emit signals at frequencies characteristic of their chemical environment.
items.why: Understanding the principle of NMR explains why chemically equivalent atoms produce the same signal, why chemical environment affects the position of peaks, and how the technique relates to the MRI technology used in medicine.
items.example: In ethanol, the carbon of the CH3 group and the carbon of the CH2OH group are in different chemical environments, so they absorb and emit radiofrequency energy at different frequencies, producing two separate peaks in the 13C NMR spectrum.

subtopic.name: Carbon-13 NMR Spectroscopy
subtopic.what: Carbon-13 NMR (13C NMR) spectroscopy measures the magnetic properties of carbon-13 nuclei in a molecule to determine how many chemically distinct carbon environments are present. Each unique carbon environment produces a peak at a characteristic chemical shift value (measured in ppm).
subtopic.why: 13C NMR provides direct structural information about the carbon skeleton of a molecule. By counting the number of peaks and comparing their chemical shifts to reference values, the number and type of different carbon environments can be identified, helping to determine molecular structure.

items.title: I can determine the number of carbon environments from a 13C NMR spectrum
items.what: Each peak in a 13C NMR spectrum corresponds to one unique carbon environment. Carbons in identical chemical environments (e.g. both CH3 groups in propane) produce a single peak, while carbons in different environments each produce a separate peak.
items.why: Counting the number of peaks tells you how many chemically distinct carbon environments are in the molecule, which is a key constraint when determining molecular structure.
items.example: Ethanol (CH3CH2OH) shows two peaks in its 13C NMR spectrum: one near 20 ppm for the CH3 carbon and one near 58 ppm for the CH2OH carbon, indicating two distinct carbon environments.

subtopic.name: Carbon-13 NMR Spectroscopy
subtopic.what: Carbon-13 NMR (13C NMR) spectroscopy measures the magnetic properties of carbon-13 nuclei in a molecule to determine how many chemically distinct carbon environments are present. Each unique carbon environment produces a peak at a characteristic chemical shift value (measured in ppm).
subtopic.why: 13C NMR provides direct structural information about the carbon skeleton of a molecule. By counting the number of peaks and comparing their chemical shifts to reference values, the number and type of different carbon environments can be identified, helping to determine molecular structure.

items.title: I can use chemical shift values to identify carbon environments in a 13C NMR spectrum
items.what: Chemical shift values (in ppm) indicate the type of carbon environment. For example, carbonyl carbons (C=O) appear at high chemical shifts (160-220 ppm), while simple alkyl carbons (R-CH3) appear at low chemical shifts (8-25 ppm).
items.why: Matching observed chemical shift values to reference ranges identifies the nature of each carbon environment, providing detailed structural information about which functional groups are present and how the carbon skeleton is arranged.
items.example: A 13C NMR spectrum showing peaks at 20 ppm and 170 ppm indicates one alkyl carbon (R-CH3, range 8-25 ppm) and one carboxyl-type carbon (RCOOH, range 160-185 ppm), consistent with ethanoic acid (CH3COOH).

subtopic.name: Carbon-13 NMR Spectroscopy
subtopic.what: Carbon-13 NMR (13C NMR) spectroscopy measures the magnetic properties of carbon-13 nuclei in a molecule to determine how many chemically distinct carbon environments are present. Each unique carbon environment produces a peak at a characteristic chemical shift value (measured in ppm).
subtopic.why: 13C NMR provides direct structural information about the carbon skeleton of a molecule. By counting the number of peaks and comparing their chemical shifts to reference values, the number and type of different carbon environments can be identified, helping to determine molecular structure.

items.title: I can determine the structure of an organic compound from given 13C NMR data
items.what: By combining the number of peaks (number of carbon environments) with the chemical shift values (types of carbon environments) and the molecular formula, you can deduce the structural formula of the compound.
items.why: This integrative skill is directly assessed in VCE and demonstrates the ability to convert raw spectral data into a structural conclusion about a real molecule.
items.example: A compound with formula C3H6O shows two 13C NMR peaks: one at 207 ppm (ketone C=O) and one at 30 ppm (R2C=O type, range 205-220 ppm). This is consistent with propanone (CH3COCH3), where both CH3 carbons are equivalent, giving only two unique environments.

subtopic.name: Carbon-13 NMR Spectroscopy
subtopic.what: Carbon-13 NMR (13C NMR) spectroscopy measures the magnetic properties of carbon-13 nuclei in a molecule to determine how many chemically distinct carbon environments are present. Each unique carbon environment produces a peak at a characteristic chemical shift value (measured in ppm).
subtopic.why: 13C NMR provides direct structural information about the carbon skeleton of a molecule. By counting the number of peaks and comparing their chemical shifts to reference values, the number and type of different carbon environments can be identified, helping to determine molecular structure.

items.title: I can use chemical shift values from a 1H NMR spectrum to identify hydrogen environments
items.what: Each distinct peak in a 1H NMR spectrum represents one unique hydrogen environment. The chemical shift value (in ppm) of each peak indicates the type of hydrogen environment, which can be identified by comparison with a reference table.
items.why: Identifying the types of hydrogen environments establishes what functional groups are present near each set of hydrogen atoms, building a picture of the molecular structure.
items.example: A peak at 9.5-10.0 ppm indicates a hydrogen attached to a carbonyl group (aldehyde, R-CHO), while a peak at 0.9-1.0 ppm indicates a hydrogen in a simple methyl group (R-CH3) attached to a carbon chain.

subtopic.name: Proton NMR Spectroscopy
subtopic.what: Proton NMR (1H NMR) spectroscopy analyses the magnetic properties of hydrogen nuclei to reveal the number, type, and arrangement of hydrogen environments in a molecule. The spectrum provides chemical shift values, integration (peak area), and in high-resolution spectra, peak splitting patterns.
subtopic.why: Proton NMR is one of the most powerful and commonly used tools in organic structure determination. It provides three layers of structural information simultaneously, and when combined with other techniques it can fully define the connectivity of atoms in complex organic molecules.

items.title: I can use integration curves to determine the relative number of protons in each environment
items.what: The area under each peak in a 1H NMR spectrum (the integration) is proportional to the number of hydrogen atoms producing that signal. Integration values are expressed as ratios to show the relative number of protons in each environment.
items.why: Integration data allows you to determine how many hydrogen atoms are in each environment, which when combined with the molecular formula helps assign specific groups (e.g. CH3 vs CH2) to each peak.
items.example: Three peaks with integration ratios of 3 : 1 : 2 in a compound with 6 hydrogens indicate environments containing 3, 1, and 2 hydrogen atoms respectively. The environment with integration 3 could correspond to a CH3 group.

subtopic.name: Proton NMR Spectroscopy
subtopic.what: Proton NMR (1H NMR) spectroscopy analyses the magnetic properties of hydrogen nuclei to reveal the number, type, and arrangement of hydrogen environments in a molecule. The spectrum provides chemical shift values, integration (peak area), and in high-resolution spectra, peak splitting patterns.
subtopic.why: Proton NMR is one of the most powerful and commonly used tools in organic structure determination. It provides three layers of structural information simultaneously, and when combined with other techniques it can fully define the connectivity of atoms in complex organic molecules.

items.title: I can apply the n+1 rule to predict and interpret peak splitting patterns
items.what: In high-resolution 1H NMR, a signal is split into n+1 peaks, where n is the number of hydrogen atoms on directly neighbouring carbon atoms. A singlet (1 peak) means no neighbouring H atoms; a doublet (2 peaks) means 1 neighbour; a triplet means 2 neighbours; a quartet means 3 neighbours.
items.why: Peak splitting reveals the number of hydrogen atoms on adjacent carbons, providing information about the connectivity of groups within the molecule. This is essential for distinguishing between structural isomers.
items.example: In ethanol (CH3CH2OH), the CH3 group has 2 neighbouring H atoms (on the adjacent CH2), so it appears as a triplet (2+1=3). The CH2 group has 3 neighbouring H atoms (on the adjacent CH3), so it appears as a quartet (3+1=4). The OH appears as a singlet.

subtopic.name: Proton NMR Spectroscopy
subtopic.what: Proton NMR (1H NMR) spectroscopy analyses the magnetic properties of hydrogen nuclei to reveal the number, type, and arrangement of hydrogen environments in a molecule. The spectrum provides chemical shift values, integration (peak area), and in high-resolution spectra, peak splitting patterns.
subtopic.why: Proton NMR is one of the most powerful and commonly used tools in organic structure determination. It provides three layers of structural information simultaneously, and when combined with other techniques it can fully define the connectivity of atoms in complex organic molecules.

items.title: I can determine the structure of an organic compound from given 1H NMR data
items.what: By combining chemical shift values (types of environments), integration ratios (number of H atoms in each environment), and peak splitting patterns (number of neighbouring H atoms), together with the molecular formula, the structural formula of the compound can be deduced.
items.why: This integrative interpretation skill is a core VCE examination requirement and represents the full analytical power of 1H NMR spectroscopy applied to a real structural problem.
items.example: A compound C4H8O2 shows three 1H NMR peaks: a triplet at 1.3 ppm (integration 3), a singlet at 2.0 ppm (integration 3), and a quartet at 4.1 ppm (integration 2). The triplet-quartet pair with 3 and 2 H atoms indicates a CH3-CH2 unit; the singlet indicates a CH3 group with no neighbours. This is consistent with ethyl ethanoate (CH3COOCH2CH3).

subtopic.name: Proton NMR Spectroscopy
subtopic.what: Proton NMR (1H NMR) spectroscopy analyses the magnetic properties of hydrogen nuclei to reveal the number, type, and arrangement of hydrogen environments in a molecule. The spectrum provides chemical shift values, integration (peak area), and in high-resolution spectra, peak splitting patterns.
subtopic.why: Proton NMR is one of the most powerful and commonly used tools in organic structure determination. It provides three layers of structural information simultaneously, and when combined with other techniques it can fully define the connectivity of atoms in complex organic molecules.

items.title: I can describe the type of structural information each spectroscopic technique provides
items.what: MS gives molecular mass and fragment masses. IR identifies functional groups (bond types). 13C NMR gives the number and types of carbon environments. 1H NMR gives the number, types, relative quantities, and connectivity of hydrogen environments.
items.why: Knowing what each technique contributes allows you to use data from each source efficiently and to recognise which technique is most useful for answering a specific structural question.
items.example: To confirm whether an unknown compound is ethanol or dimethyl ether (both C2H6O), MS gives the same molecular mass (46) for both, but IR distinguishes them: only ethanol shows a broad O-H absorption at 3200-3600 cm-1, while dimethyl ether shows a C-O absorption but no O-H.

subtopic.name: Combined Spectral Analysis
subtopic.what: Combined spectral analysis involves using data from mass spectrometry (MS), infrared spectroscopy (IR), carbon-13 NMR, and proton NMR together to determine the structure of an unknown organic compound. Each technique provides complementary information that, when combined, allows for a definitive structural determination.
subtopic.why: No single analytical technique can provide complete structural information about an unknown compound. Using multiple techniques together is standard practice in research and industry, and is a central skill assessed in VCE Chemistry Unit 4.

items.title: I can use MS data as a starting point to determine molecular mass and possible molecular formulas
items.what: The molecular ion peak in the MS spectrum gives the molecular mass directly. This value is used to calculate or confirm the molecular formula of the compound, which then constrains all subsequent spectral interpretation.
items.why: The molecular formula defines what elements and how many atoms are present, setting the boundary conditions for all structural possibilities before any other spectral data is considered.
items.example: An unknown compound shows a molecular ion peak at m/z = 74. If told the empirical formula is C2H5O, the molecular formula must be C4H10O2 (M = 90), which does not match. If the empirical formula is C3H6O, the molecular formula is C3H6O (M = 58), which also does not match m/z = 74, so the correct formula must be recalculated.

subtopic.name: Combined Spectral Analysis
subtopic.what: Combined spectral analysis involves using data from mass spectrometry (MS), infrared spectroscopy (IR), carbon-13 NMR, and proton NMR together to determine the structure of an unknown organic compound. Each technique provides complementary information that, when combined, allows for a definitive structural determination.
subtopic.why: No single analytical technique can provide complete structural information about an unknown compound. Using multiple techniques together is standard practice in research and industry, and is a central skill assessed in VCE Chemistry Unit 4.

items.title: I can determine the structure of an organic compound by combining MS, IR, and NMR data
items.what: A systematic approach is used: first determine molecular mass from MS, then identify functional groups from IR, then determine the number and type of carbon environments from 13C NMR, and finally use 1H NMR chemical shifts, integration, and splitting patterns to establish the complete structure.
items.why: This combined approach is the most powerful method of structure determination available without X-ray crystallography and directly mirrors professional practice in pharmaceutical, forensic, and research chemistry.
items.example: An unknown compound (C4H8O): MS shows M = 72. IR shows a strong C=O trough near 1715 cm-1 (ketone) and no O-H. 13C NMR shows 3 peaks. 1H NMR shows two environments in a 3:1 ratio at 2.1 ppm (singlet) and 1.3 ppm. The data is consistent with butanone (CH3COCH2CH3)... continuing refinement with splitting data would confirm or revise this.

Each technique provides complementary information that, when combined, allows for a definitive structural determination.
subtopic.why: No single analytical technique can provide complete structural information about an unknown compound. Using multiple techniques together is standard practice in research and industry, and is a central skill assessed in VCE Chemistry Unit 4.

items.title: I can describe the principle of high-performance liquid chromatography
items.what: In HPLC, a sample is injected into a column containing a stationary phase. A liquid mobile phase flows through the column, carrying the sample components. Each component interacts with the stationary phase to a different degree, causing them to travel through the column at different speeds and elute at different times.
items.why: Understanding the principle of separation is essential for predicting the order of elution of different compounds and for interpreting chromatogram data correctly in terms of polarity and intermolecular interactions.
items.example: Using a polar silica stationary phase and a non-polar hexane mobile phase, a polar compound like ethanoic acid interacts strongly with the stationary phase and has a long retention time, while a non-polar compound like hexane interacts weakly and elutes quickly.

subtopic.name: HPLC Chromatography
subtopic.what: High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) separates the components of a mixture by passing a liquid mobile phase through a column packed with a solid stationary phase. Components interact differently with the stationary phase and elute at different times, called retention times, which are detected to produce a chromatogram.
subtopic.why: HPLC is used extensively in pharmaceutical quality control, environmental monitoring, food science, and forensic analysis to separate, identify, and quantify organic compounds in complex mixtures. It provides quantitative data about concentration through the use of calibration curves.

items.title: I can describe the roles of the stationary phase and mobile phase in HPLC
items.what: The stationary phase remains fixed in the column and interacts with sample components to slow their passage. The mobile phase is the liquid that flows through the column, carrying the sample and competing with the stationary phase for interactions with the sample components.
items.why: Understanding the roles of each phase allows you to predict how changes to the stationary or mobile phase will affect the separation and retention times of different compounds.
items.example: In a reverse-phase HPLC system, the stationary phase is non-polar (e.g. a C18 hydrocarbon chain) and the mobile phase is polar (e.g. water-methanol). Non-polar compounds interact more with the stationary phase and have longer retention times; polar compounds elute first.

subtopic.name: HPLC Chromatography
subtopic.what: High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) separates the components of a mixture by passing a liquid mobile phase through a column packed with a solid stationary phase. Components interact differently with the stationary phase and elute at different times, called retention times, which are detected to produce a chromatogram.
subtopic.why: HPLC is used extensively in pharmaceutical quality control, environmental monitoring, food science, and forensic analysis to separate, identify, and quantify organic compounds in complex mixtures. It provides quantitative data about concentration through the use of calibration curves.

items.title: I can use retention times from HPLC data to help identify organic compounds
items.what: A compound always has the same retention time when run under identical conditions (same column, same mobile phase, same temperature). By comparing the retention time of an unknown peak with that of a known standard run under the same conditions, a tentative identification can be made.
items.why: Retention time matching is the primary qualitative identification method in HPLC. However, because different compounds can share the same retention time, it provides an indication of identity rather than a definitive confirmation.
items.example: A pure vitamin C standard run on a specific HPLC column produces a peak at Rt = 3.2 minutes. A multivitamin sample run on the same column under the same conditions also shows a peak at Rt = 3.2 minutes, suggesting vitamin C is present in the multivitamin.

subtopic.name: HPLC Chromatography
subtopic.what: High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) separates the components of a mixture by passing a liquid mobile phase through a column packed with a solid stationary phase. Components interact differently with the stationary phase and elute at different times, called retention times, which are detected to produce a chromatogram.
subtopic.why: HPLC is used extensively in pharmaceutical quality control, environmental monitoring, food science, and forensic analysis to separate, identify, and quantify organic compounds in complex mixtures. It provides quantitative data about concentration through the use of calibration curves.

items.title: I can describe the qualitative purity of a substance from given HPLC data
items.what: A pure single-component sample produces only one peak on the chromatogram at the expected retention time. Additional peaks indicate the presence of impurities or contaminants. Peaks at unexpected retention times suggest the presence of unintended substances.
items.why: Assessing purity is a critical application of HPLC in pharmaceutical manufacturing and chemical synthesis. Confirming that a product shows only the expected peak(s) provides evidence that the synthesis was successful and the product is sufficiently pure.
items.example: A pharmaceutical company synthesises aspirin and runs a sample on HPLC. A pure sample should show one peak at the expected retention time for aspirin. If a second peak appears at a different retention time, this indicates an impurity is present, and the batch may not meet purity standards.

subtopic.what: High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) separates the components of a mixture by passing a liquid mobile phase through a column packed with a solid stationary phase. Components interact differently with the stationary phase and elute at different times, called retention times, which are detected to produce a chromatogram.
subtopic.why: HPLC is used extensively in pharmaceutical quality control, environmental monitoring, food science, and forensic analysis to separate, identify, and quantify organic compounds in complex mixtures. It provides quantitative data about concentration through the use of calibration curves.

items.title: I can construct a calibration curve from given HPLC data
items.what: A calibration curve is constructed by plotting the peak area (y-axis) against the known concentration of a series of standard solutions (x-axis), then drawing a line of best fit through the data points. The curve establishes a linear relationship between concentration and detector response.
items.why: The calibration curve is the tool that converts a raw instrument measurement (peak area) into a meaningful concentration value for an unknown sample. It accounts for the specific instrument conditions used and ensures accurate quantification.
items.example: Standards of phenol at concentrations 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, and 0.5 g/L produce peak areas of 103, 198, 304, 410, and 497 respectively. Plotting peak area versus concentration and drawing a line of best fit produces a calibration curve with a linear relationship.

subtopic.name: HPLC Chromatography
subtopic.what: High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) separates the components of a mixture by passing a liquid mobile phase through a column packed with a solid stationary phase. Components interact differently with the stationary phase and elute at different times, called retention times, which are detected to produce a chromatogram.
subtopic.why: HPLC is used extensively in pharmaceutical quality control, environmental monitoring, food science, and forensic analysis to separate, identify, and quantify organic compounds in complex mixtures. It provides quantitative data about concentration through the use of calibration curves.

items.title: I can calculate the concentration of an organic compound from a calibration curve and HPLC data
items.what: To find the concentration of an unknown sample, calculate the average peak area from replicate injections, then locate this value on the y-axis of the calibration curve, draw a horizontal line to the line of best fit, and drop a vertical line to the x-axis to read off the concentration. Account for any dilution factors used in sample preparation.
items.why: Quantitative determination of concentration is one of the most important practical applications of HPLC, used in environmental testing, food safety, pharmacokinetics, and quality control to ensure compounds are present at safe and effective levels.
items.example: Three creek water samples produce average peak area of 179 on an HPLC calibrated with phenol standards. Reading across from peak area 179 on the y-axis to the calibration line, then down to the x-axis, gives a concentration of 0.175 g/L in the diluted sample. If the sample was diluted 10-fold, the original creek water concentration is 1.75 g/L.
